papers.title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure.

The authors conclude that physiological manipulation of cortical activity can dissociate ER-stress molecular signatures from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure.

papers.title: Neural circuitry mediating hypercapnia-induced microarousal and impaired sleep depth.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption in obstructive sleep apnea syndrome is characterized by frequent microarousals and reduced sleep depth, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that intermittent hypercapnic air (HA) induces time-locked microarousals, fragments sleep, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep depth, and diminishes rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. HA exposure activates glutamatergic neurons in the nucleus tract solitary (NTSVglut2), and their optogenetic or chemogenetic activation is sufficient to trigger arousal and impair sleep. Projection-specific activation reveals that NTSVglut2 projections to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN), parabrachial nucleus (PB), paraventricular thalamus, and locus coeruleus (LC) promote arousal, whereas projections to the PB and LC additionally reduce NREM sleep depth. Inhibition of NTSVglut2 projection to the PVN significantly postpones HA-induced arousal. NTSVglut2 terminals monosynaptically activate corticotropin-releasing hormone neurons in the PVN (PVNCRH), and inhibition of PVNCRH neurons or knockdown of Slc17a6 (encoding Vglut2), but not Crh, delays hypercapnia-induced arousal. These findings identify neural circuits underlying hypercapnia-induced microarousal and reduced sleep depth.

papers.title: ppGpp is present in, and functions to regulate sleep of, Drosophila.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for animals, and receives inputs from circadian, homeostasis, and environment, yet the mechanisms of sleep regulation remain elusive. Discovery of molecules in living systems and demonstration of their functional roles are pivotal in furthering our understanding of the molecular basis of biology. Here, we report that guanosine-5'-diphosphate, 3'-diphosphate (ppGpp) is present in Drosophila, and plays an important role in regulation of sleep and starvation-induced sleep loss (SISL). ppGpp is detected in germ-free Drosophila and hydrolyzed by an enzyme encoded by the mesh1 gene in Drosophila. Nighttime sleep and SISL were defected in mesh1 mutant flies, and rescued by expression of wildtype Mesh1, but not the enzymatically defective mutant Mesh1E66A. Ectopic expression of RelA, the Escherichia coli synthetase for ppGpp, phenocopied mesh1 knockout mutants, whereas overexpression of Mesh1 resulted in the opposite phenotypes, supporting that ppGpp is both necessary and sufficient in sleep regulation. A chemo connectomic screen followed by genetic intersection experiments implicates the Dilp2 neurons in the pars intercerebralis (PI) brain region as the site of ppGpp function. Our results have thus validated the presence of ppGpp in Drosophila and revealed a physiological role of ppGpp in sleep regulation for the first time.

papers.title: "Frontal Slow-Wave Asymmetry in Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Its Modulation During CPAP Titration".
papers.abstract: Sleep slow-wave activity (SWA) shows regional and hemispheric variation reflecting local cortical regulation. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) introduces recurrent respiratory instability and arousals that may alter cortical dynamics during sleep. It remains unclear whether continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) affects hemispheric SWA balance. In this retrospective observational study, we included adult patients who underwent diagnostic polysomnography followed by a CPAP titration study on a separate night. Frontal delta power during N3 sleep was calculated from F3-A2 and F4-A1 using spectral analysis. Hemispheric asymmetry was quantified using a normalized asymmetry index (F4 - F3) / (F4 + F3). Sleep, respiratory, and EEG parameters were compared using paired nonparametric tests. A total of 143 patients were included (median age 47 years, 76% male). CPAP improved respiratory parameters, with median apnea-hypopnea index decreasing from 27.4 to 3.2 events/h (P < .001). Frontal delta power decreased at both F3 and F4 during CPAP (P < .001). Absolute asymmetry index decreased from 9.35% to 7.55% (P = .008). Signed asymmetry shifted toward left hemispheric dominance (P < .001). Right-dominant patterns were more frequent during the diagnostic night, whereas left-dominant patterns predominated during CPAP. Among patients with non-neutral asymmetry on both nights, dominance direction changed significantly (McNemar P = .008), mainly from right to left. CPAP is associated with reduced frontal delta power and attenuation of hemispheric SWA asymmetry during deep sleep, suggesting that respiratory stabilization may influence cortical organization. These findings should be interpreted considering potential night-to-night effects.

papers.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
papers.abstract: SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.

It also reproduced awake spectral abnormalities and revealed sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics.

papers.title: From labels to latents: revealing state-dependent hippocampal computations and non-spatial replay with Jump Latent Variable Model
papers.abstract: Neural activity is often interpreted by imposing external labels (e.g., position during locomotion) and decoding within that space (e.g. replay). While powerful, such supervision can mask structure in the data that do not correspond to the label. Unsupervised methods, in turn, often assume smooth latent dynamics and miss genuine discontinuities. We introduce a conceptually simple, computationally efficient latent variable model that infers both (i) the latent variables organizing population activity and (ii) whether their dynamics are continuous or fragmented in time. Fitting reduces to an expectation-maximization (EM) procedure that alternates two operations familiar to systems neuroscience - tuning-curve estimation and label decoding - without requiring external labels. Applied to rodent hippocampal recordings, our method identifies a continuity-fragmentation axis that characterizes population activity across sleep-wake brain states, modulated by cholinergic inputs. For a spatial navigation task, the model reveals distinct population patterns at the same physical position that supervised spatial decoding fails to detect. Moreover, the model enables replay analysis beyond spatial trajectories, and finds prevalent pre-play events associated with immobile and off-maze behaviors and post-task replay of locomotion. By not relying on externally imposed spatial labels, our approach exposes structure that supervised approaches obscure and provides a powerful tool for datasets lacking behavioral tracking.

Applied to rodent hippocampus, it identifies a cholinergic-modulated continuity-fragmentation axis across sleep-wake states, reveals position-independent population patterns missed by supervised spatial decoding, and uncovers prevalent non-spatial pre-play and post-task locomotor replay.

papers.title: Associations Between Biomarkers of Alzheimer's Disease and Sleep in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances have been implicated as a risk factor for developing Alzheimer's disease (AD), but evidence linking plasma AD biomarkers to sleep in cognitively unimpaired individuals remains limited. The present study examined associations between evening, morning, and overnight changes in plasma AD biomarkers and measures of sleep macro- and microstructure and subjective sleep quality in older adults. Forty cognitively unimpaired adults aged 55 to 75 years (20 females) without sleep or mental disorders underwent overnight polysomnography. Plasma AD biomarkers p-tau181, p-tau217, t-tau, Aβ42, Aβ40, and Aβ42/40 were assessed in the evening and in the morning and related to sleep macro- and microstructure (sleep spindles, EEG spectral power), and subjective sleep measures by using correlational analyzes. Higher evening t-tau and p-tau181 were associated with reduced N3 sleep, whereas higher morning t-tau and greater overnight increases in t-tau were related to longer nocturnal wakefulness. Amyloid-β measures showed the most consistent associations with sleep microstructure. Higher Aβ42 and Aβ40 concentrations were associated with shorter duration and lower density of sleep spindles, particularly at frontal sites. Higher evening and morning amyloid-β concentrations were also associated with lower alpha, beta, and spindle-frequency EEG power, mainly during non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tau associations with EEG spectral power were less consistent. In cognitively unimpaired older adults, plasma AD biomarkers were associated with PSG sleep features, especially amyloid-β markers with sleep microstructure. These exploratory, correlational findings suggest that sleep spindles and spectral power may reflect early AD-related biological processes but require replication in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Sequential coupling of sleep oscillations enables concept-neuron reactivation and supports information flow across the human hippocampal-cortical circuit
papers.abstract: Effective memory consolidation during sleep is thought to rely on the transfer of reactivated memory traces from the hippocampus to the cortex. However, the mechanisms supporting this essential dialogue across brain areas remain poorly understood. Here, we recorded single-neuron activity (n = 1097) in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) of 10 epilepsy patients across 21 nights of sleep. Before sleep, patients engaged in a memory task with stimuli eliciting concept-neuron responses. During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, neuronal firing locked to sharp wave-ripples (SWR) revealed a directed flow of information from the hippocampus to cortical targets. Notably, within SWR-driven activity, experience-dependent concept neurons exhibited elevated co-activation both within and across MTL regions, indicating selective reactivation of behaviorally relevant information. Cross-regional co-activation of concept cells was markedly enhanced when hippocampal SWRs coincided with cortical slow oscillation-spindle complexes, suggesting an active role of the cortex in shaping interregional communication. These findings provide evidence that SWRs in humans selectively reactivate experience-related neural ensembles across the hippocampal-cortical network, while synergistic interactions with cortical slow oscillation-spindle events might facilitate effective memory consolidation.

papers.title: Circadian rhythms in health and disease.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms, serving as a crucial temporal bridge linking neural activity and pathological biology, are regulated by central pacemaker neurons to maintain cellular homeostasis and coordinate diverse biological processes. Circadian rhythm disruption is closely associated with various diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Circadian rhythms are controlled by core clock genes, such as BMAL1 and CLOCK, modulating numerous physiological processes, encompassing metabolism, immune responses, neural activity, and hormone regulation. Circadian rhythms disruptions arising from shift work, jet lag, or inconsistent sleep schedules are implicated in both the onset and progression of numerous diseases, notably Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The article highlights how circadian dysregulation alters cellular processes to potentially accelerate disease progression. Circadian disruption results in impaired immune function, further promoting disease development and resistance to treatment. Potential therapeutic applications based on circadian biology, such as chronotherapy and personalized medicine, are also discussed. Recent technological advances, embodied in wearable devices and omics approaches, are increasingly providing deeper insights into circadian biology. Further unveiling the role of circadian in health and disease opens new avenues for tailoring treatment timing to patients' biological rhythms, thereby enhancing therapeutic outcomes across various diseases. By bridging fundamental circadian mechanisms with clinical pathology, this review provides a roadmap for future chronotherapeutic interventions in precision medicine.

papers.title: Framework for combined functional and computational assessment of variant pathogenicity in the sodium leak channel NALCN.
papers.abstract: The sodium leak channel nonselective (NALCN) is the pore-forming channel component of the NALCN channelosome. This protein complex generates a depolarizing sodium leak in various tissues and contributes to respiratory and circadian rhythms, locomotion, and sleep. De novo and inherited variants of NALCN can lead to severe developmental syndromes referred to as CLIFAHDD and IHPRF1, respectively. Although variants of uncertain significance (VUS) have been studied in heterologous expression systems before, there is no generally accepted framework for how to assess or predict variant pathogenicity. We functionally and computationally characterize 19 VUS detected in CLIFAHDD and IHPRF1 patients to establish a robust analysis to classify suspected disease-causing variants. Specifically, we employ multiple parameters derived from two-electrode voltage-clamp electrophysiology recordings and predicted protein stability and conservation scores. We show that this approach is capable of distinguishing benign common variants from both gain- and loss-of-function (GoF/LoF) variants. Additionally, our work provides insight into the molecular mechanism underlying specific variants and the unusual propensity of NALCN missense variants to result in GoF phenotypes. We anticipate that this experimental and computational framework will aid assessment of variant pathogenicity of NALCN and other components of the channelosome in the future.

papers.title: Advances in neurological disease models and optimization of the laboratory animal environment for reproducible research.
papers.abstract: Animal models of neurological diseases have evolved from phenotype-based systems to integrated platforms that link genetics, molecular signaling, synaptic physiology, neural circuits, behavior, and therapeutic responses. Simultaneously, increasingly precise phenotyping has revealed that experimental outcomes are strongly influenced by age, microbiological status, diet, housing, stress, previous experience, health status, and measurement methodology. This review considers these two developments to be complementary requirements for reliable experimental neuroscience. Studies on voltage-gated calcium channel mutants have shown that defined genetic alterations can produce age-dependent abnormalities in motor function, cognition, emotion, autonomic regulation, and seizure susceptibility. Studies on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor-Calcium-calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) signaling, epigenetic regulators, stress-related phenotypes, and fear memory circuits have further illustrated how animal models can be characterized across levels, from molecular mechanisms to neural ensembles and therapeutic rescues. Translation to common marmosets extends these approaches to primate sleep and epilepsy, while highlighting the effects of genetic diversity, spontaneous disease, handling, and colony management. In parallel, studies on germ-free animals, diet, the gut microbiota, barrier facilities, cage enrichment, telemetry, and veterinary monitoring have demonstrated that husbandry variables, rather than technical background, are biological determinants. Integrating rigorous disease model characterization with evidence-based husbandry, environmental control, and transparent reporting should improve the reproducibility and translational value of preclinical neuroscience research and the welfare of the animals used.

papers.title: Longitudinal Sleep Spindle Maturation Trajectories and Their Association With Internalizing Problems in Adulthood.
papers.abstract: Extensive cortical refinement from childhood to adulthood coincides with heightened vulnerability to internalizing problems, such as anxiety and depression. Thalamocortical sleep spindles may provide neurophysiological indices of such vulnerability. In this longitudinal study (2009-2023), we examined developmental trajectories of slow (11-13 Hz) and fast (13-15 Hz) spindle density across childhood (≈9.5 years), adolescence (≈16 years) and young adulthood (≈22.5 years), and tested whether individual differences in these trajectories were associated with internalizing problems during adulthood. At each wave, participants completed two nights of ambulatory polysomnography (N = 28; 19 female). Internalizing problems were assessed using five standardized self-report and external-report questionnaires. Slow spindle density declined between childhood and adulthood, with a posterior-to-anterior pattern characterized by earlier centroparietal and later frontal reductions. Fast spindle density globally increased from childhood to adolescence and then stabilized. Associations with internalizing problems were specific to slow spindle development: more internalizing problems were linked to a steeper decline in widespread slow spindle density from childhood to adolescence. Because questionnaire measures showed no evidence of developmental change in our sample, this association reflects interindividual differences rather than symptom emergence. These findings indicate that a steeper decline in slow spindle density from childhood to adolescence is associated with more internalizing problems, underscoring the importance of a developmental perspective when linking sleep spindles to emotional functioning.

papers.title: Decoding Cell-level Circadian Phase and Rhythm-state Remodeling in Single-cell Transcriptomes With scRhythmBayes
papers.abstract: Current circadian omics analysis tools have been developed primarily for bulk time-series. However, heterogeneous single-cell datasets require analysis and interpretation of rhythmic programs across different cells, cell types, and biological conditions. In these datasets, cellular circadian phase is usually unobserved, and sample-level zeitgeber time provides temporal information but does not define the exact phase of every cell. Existing methods address only selected aspects of this problem and do not model how cell-level phase evidence informs gene-level rhythmic parameters and rhythm-state remodeling. Here we present scRhythmBayes, a new probabilistic algorithm for phase-resolved circadian analysis in heterogeneous single-cell transcriptomes. scRhythmBayes combines a seed-gene count likelihood with a stratum-aware circular prior to infer cell-level circadian phase, incorporates phase support into gene-level rhythmic modeling, and assigns posterior probabilities to interpretable rhythm-state categories, including rhythm gain, rhythm loss, amplitude remodeling and phase shifts. In heterogeneous simulations, scRhythmBayes achieved higher phase-recovery accuracy than existing phase-inference methods and maintained balanced performance across rhythmic gene detection, parameter recovery, and rhythm-state classification. Stress tests defined practical requirements for seed-gene support, zeitgeber anchoring, temporal sampling density, and cell number. In mouse liver, scRhythmBayes revealed distinct circadian phase occupancy and rhythm-state organization between periportal and pericentral hepatocytes, supporting a temporal dimension of liver zonation. It also identified cell-type-specific rhythmic markers that were largely distinct from conventional static markers, indicating that cellular identity includes temporal programs not captured by average expression. In human heart disease data, phase-coordination and phase-distribution analyses identified cell-type-selective temporal disorganization rather than uniform circadian disruption across the tissue. scRhythmBayes therefore provides a statistically grounded approach for resolving circadian organization across cells, genes, cell types and biological conditions.

papers.title: It's about time: modeling circadian regulation of cardiac electrophysiology and arrhythmogenesis.
papers.abstract: Cardiac electrophysiology models resolve processes ranging from millisecond-scale ion-channel gating to hour-scale protein trafficking; yet, most do not explicitly represent circadian time. Consequently, ion-channel conductance, autonomic input, body temperature, and clock-regulated gene expression are often treated as fixed parameters or time-invariant inputs, causing simulated cardiac cells to correspond to an implicit and potentially arbitrary biological phase. In vivo, however, these factors vary across the ∼24-h cycle and jointly shape sinoatrial nodal pacemaking, ventricular repolarization, arrhythmia susceptibility, and drug response. In this mini-review, we examine recent efforts to incorporate circadian regulation into computational models of cardiac electrophysiology, including sinoatrial nodal and ventricular myocyte models of pacemaking, arrhythmogenesis, seizure-induced sinus arrhythmias, and drug-induced proarrhythmic risk. We synthesize these studies using a layered "source-transfer-target" organization in which intrinsic and systemic circadian sources act through source-specific transfer processes-including transcription, translation, channel trafficking, receptor-mediated signaling, and direct thermal modulation-to regulate shared electrophysiological targets. Building on this synthesis, we propose a general current-level formulation for incorporating circadian regulation of maximal conductance, channel gating, and ionic driving force into Hodgkin-Huxley-type models. Finally, we identify the experimental, computational, and clinical advances needed to translate these formulations into human-specific, personalized models of cardiac rhythm and arrhythmogenesis, with the long-term goal of enabling circadian-aware cardiac digital twins for time-resolved risk prediction and chronotherapeutic optimization.

papers.title: Glycosides of Cistanche improve cognitive dysfunction in sleep-deprived model rats by activating the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation suppresses the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway, leading to oxidative stress, synaptic damage, and cognitive dysfunction. Glycosides of Cistanche (GCs) possess well-documented antioxidant and neuroprotective properties and have been reported to improve cognition in sleep-deprived animals, but the molecular mechanism remains unclear. We hypothesized that GCs alleviate sleep deprivation-induced cognitive dysfunction by activating the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway. Sixty male Sprague Dawley rats were randomly assigned to six groups (n = 10): Control, Platform, Model, GCs, Control+GCs, and Estazolam (Est) groups. A 21-day sleep deprivation model was established using the modified multiple platform water method. Assessments included cognitive function by Morris water maze (MWM) test; Wake, non-rapid eye movement (NREM), rapid eye movement (REM), and total sleep time (TST) by Electroencephalogram (EEG); the serum levels of MDA, GSH-Px and SOD by ELISA, hippocampal CA1 neuronal morphology structure by Nissl staining and transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway and synaptic related proteins were detected by Western blot. In an additional cohort (n = 40), the SIRT1-specific inhibitor EX527 was used to validate the causal role of the pathway. Compared with the Control group, the Model group exhibited significantly prolonged escape latency, along with reduced the number of platform crossings and the percentage time in the target quadrant (p < 0.05). The proportion of Wake significantly increased, while NREM, REM, and TST all significantly decreased (all p < 0.01). The serum level of MDA elevated, while GSH-Px and SOD activities markedly reduced (all p < 0.01). Hippocampal CA1 neurons showed disorganized arrangement, decreased Nissl bodies, and mitochondrial damage. Moreover, the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway and synaptic related proteins significantly downregulated (all p < 0.01). Nevertheless, GCs intervention ameliorated cognitive dysfunction, alleviated oxidative stress and neuronal damage, and upregulated the protein expression levels above mentioned (all p < 0.01). Notably, these protective effects of GCs were abrogated by the SIRT1 inhibitor EX527. GCs inhibited oxidative stress damage and improved synaptic plasticity, and thereby alleviated sleep deprivation induced cognitive dysfunction by activating the SIRT1/PGC-1α/Nrf2 signaling pathway.

papers.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction Across Sleep Disorders and Its Cognitive Implications
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), sleep deprivation (SD), and narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), are associated with cognitive dysfunction and an increased risk of neurodegenerative disease. Glymphatic transport disruption has been suggested as one potential mechanistic link. However, evidence across sleep disorders and glymphatic-related metrics remains fragmented. We aimed to determine whether glymphatic-related metrics are altered in OSA, SD, and NT1. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical and preclinical studies to determine whether glymphatic-related metrics are altered in OSA, SD, and NT1. Across studies of OSA, glymphatic-related metrics indicated significant impairment of glymphatic transport with a moderate negative association between apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index (r=-0.53, 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.63 to -0.41; p<0.001). Available evidence did not demonstrate statistically significant alterations in glymphatic measures in SD or NT1. These findings suggest that impaired glymphatic transport may represent a potential pathway linking OSA to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative risk. However, current evidence is insufficient to determine whether comparable alterations occur in SD or NT1. Substantial heterogeneity across studies highlights the need for standardized reporting and harmonized methodologies to advance the field.

papers.title: EEG-Captioner: Grounding EEG-to-Language Generation in Fundamental Signal Properties
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-to-language models offer a promising approach for translating complex neural signals into human-readable descriptions. However, generating plausible language does not necessarily demonstrate that a model has learned to interpret the underlying EEG signal. A direct way to assess such interpretation is to probe objectively measurable properties of the signal itself. We therefore construct an EEG-language dataset of 160,781 segments annotated with signal-level question answering (QA) pairs, where each question targets one of five property families and requires a quantitative comparison involving spectral, spatial, temporal, or lateral signal properties. Each segment is also paired with a feature-grounded EEG caption. We further propose a Dual-Domain EEG Encoder that jointly models temporal waveforms and spectral-spatial representations, and introduce EEG-Captioner, a unified EEG-to-language framework trained with both signal-level QA and EEG caption supervision. Experiments show that the proposed encoder achieves the highest overall macro-averaged balanced accuracy (Macro-BA) among the compared EEG encoders, while EEG-Captioner achieves a Macro-BA of 88.81% on signal-level QA and improves caption factual consistency from 82.06% to 83.46% over caption-only language adaptation, demonstrating the complementary benefits of signal-level QA and caption supervision.

papers.title: Neural responses to food-related stimuli following experimental sleep manipulation: A systematic review of task-based neuroimaging studies.
papers.abstract: Adequate sleep is essential for physiological, cognitive, and mental functioning. While epidemiological and behavioral studies show that sleep restriction or sleep deprivation is associated with altered responses to food stimuli, the neural mechanisms underlying these effects remain unclear. The preregistered systematic review synthesized evidence from task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging studies examining neural responses to food-related stimuli following experimental sleep manipulations, including sleep deprivation or sleep restriction. Literature searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and American Psychological Association PsycInfo, yielding 11 eligible studies, including nine with adult samples and two with adolescent samples. We extracted the data, assessed the risk of bias, and conducted a qualitative synthesis. Across studies with adult samples, six visual food-cue studies generally reported stronger brain activity following sleep deprivation or sleep restriction, particularly in the striatum, insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and inferior frontal gyrus. Two food valuation studies, including a willingness-to-pay and food-desire task, showed enhanced neural activity in the amygdala and hypothalamus during food valuation. Moreover, one study using a food odor perception paradigm showed that sleep deprivation altered chemosensory and interoceptive processing by enhancing food odor encoding in the piriform cortex. Two adolescent studies reported distinct neural findings. Together, these findings highlight that experimentally induced sleep deprivation or sleep restriction does not uniformly enhance reward-related brain activity; rather, it is associated with task-dependent changes in neural responses to food-related stimuli. However, the limited and heterogeneous evidence limits conclusions regarding common neural mechanisms. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Acute creatine-guanidinoacetate supplementation improves regional brain oxygenation following sleep deprivation: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep deprivation impairs cognitive performance and may alter regional cerebral oxygenation. Nutritional strategies that preserve brain oxygenation could help mitigate these adverse effects. Aim: To compare the acute effects of creatine-guanidinoacetate (GAA), molecular hydrogen inhalation, caffeine, and placebo on regional brain oxygenation and attention-related performance following sleep deprivation.Methods: Twenty-two healthy young adults completed a 24-hour sleep deprivation protocol and were randomly assigned to receive creatine-GAA, molecular hydrogen inhalation, caffeine, or placebo. Brain oxygenation was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy over the frontal, temporal, and occipital cortices during a modified attention network test. Alertness, executive control, orienting, reaction time, and accuracy were also evaluated.Summary: Creatine-GAA significantly increased frontal oxygen saturation (50.8% ± 4.1% to 61.0% ± 5.9%, P = 0.01; Cohen's d = 2.00) and temporal oxygen saturation (63.1% ± 4.8% to 70.2% ± 2.6%, P = 0.01; Cohen's d = 1.83). Significant time-by-treatment interactions were observed for frontal oxygen saturation (P = 0.043; ηp2 = 0.331), temporal oxygen saturation (P = 0.021; ηp2 = 0.428), and occipital total hemoglobin (P = 0.022; ηp2 = 0.405). No significant between-group differences were observed in attention-related outcomes. Acute creatine-GAA supplementation improved regional brain oxygenation following sleep deprivation, particularly in the frontal and temporal cortices, without measurable improvements in attention-related performance. These preliminary findings support further investigation of creatine-based nutritional strategies in larger randomized controlled trials.

papers.title: Impaired Dynamic Cerebral Autoregulation Across the REM Sleep Behavior Disorder Spectrum: Evidence From Isolated REM Sleep Without Atonia to Parkinson's Disease With RBD.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by REM sleep without atonia (RSWA) and dream-enactment behaviors and is recognized as a prodromal manifestation of α-synucleinopathies. Isolated RSWA (iRSWA) has been proposed as a potential early stage within the RBD spectrum, although its clinical and physiological significance remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate alterations in sleep architecture, phasic muscle activity, and dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA) across the spectrum from iRSWA to isolated RBD (iRBD) and Parkinson's disease with RBD (PD + RBD). We conducted a case-control study involving patients with iRSWA, iRBD, and PD + RBD, as well as age- and sex-matched healthy controls, based on video-polysomnography and magnetic resonance imaging. Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's Disease-Autonomic Dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT) were used to evaluate the autonomic function. Transcranial Doppler and finger plethysmography were used to assess dCA by analyzing the phase difference using transfer function analysis. A total of 25 patients with iRSWA, 30 with iRBD, 28 with PD + RBD, and 30 healthy controls were included. REM sleep percentage was significantly lower in the iRBD and PD + RBD groups than in controls. Phasic RSWA, but not tonic RSWA, differed significantly among the three patient groups (p < 0.001). Phase difference was significantly lower in all three patient groups than in controls (p < 0.001) and was significantly associated with REM sleep amount and phasic RSWA (both p < 0.001). These findings suggest that dCA is impaired in patients with iRSWA, iRBD, and PD + RBD. Reduced phase difference was associated with lower REM sleep amount and greater phasic RSWA, suggesting disrupted coupling among REM sleep regulation, autonomic function, and cerebrovascular control. dCA dysfunction may represent an early pathophysiological feature in RBD-related neurodegeneration. papers.title: EEG Edge-Centric Dynamics Reveal Distinct Post-Stroke Somatosensory Network Responses to Vibratory and Electrical Stimulation.
papers.abstract: Stroke-induced somatosensory deficits disrupt sensorimotor integration (SMI) and limit motor recovery, yet the immediate network-level effects of different somatosensory interventions remain unclear, hindering patient-specific rehabilitation planning. We propose an informatics framework based on edge-centric dynamic connectivity (ECDC) to characterize transient, whole-brain EEG network responses to sensory-level focal vibratory stimulation (FVS) and neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES). We analyzed EEG recordings from 15 chronic stroke participants and 15 healthy controls during forearm stimulation and quantified temporal network dynamics, spectral network organization, and interhemispheric interactions from instantaneous overlapping functional networks. Compared with NMES, FVS in stroke participants induced a distinct neurophysiological profile, including (i) shorter global theta-network latency, suggesting faster attentional engagement; (ii) higher contralesional alpha network diversity, indicating enhanced somatosensory recruitment; and (iii) reduced theta-alpha phase-amplitude coupling, reflecting decoupled interhemispheric interactions that may support adaptive reorganization. These findings provide interpretable network signatures for differentiating stimulation-specific brain responses and suggest a data driven route toward personalized SMI rehabilitation.

papers.title: Decoding motor imagery EEG signals by a deep learning network integrating multiscale filtering and temporal-channel attention mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Due to their low signal-to-noise ratio and non-stationarity, accurately classifying EEG signals is still one of the main hindrances that limit the real-world applications of a brain-computer interface (BCI). Deep learning (DL) is a potential method for addressing the problem. However, how to create a suitable DL network for motor imagery (MI)-based BCIs poses severe challenges in the case of insufficient training data. In this paper, a DL network based on multiscale convolutional neural network (CNN) and temporal and channel attention mechanisms is proposed for decoding MI tasks. Temporal and spatial features are extracted by four parallel CNN branches, each of which is followed by a Transformer block for learning the global correlations of local time features. The outputs from the four Transformer blocks are concatenated along channel dimension and then input into a channel attention module for channel fusion. The subsequent feature map is classified by a CNN, which replaces the commonly used fully connected layer for reducing computational complexity. The proposed network was evaluated on three publicly available BCI datasets and compared with five state-of-the-art DL networks. The training data sets are augmented using the approach segmentation and reconstruction. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed network achieved an average accuracy of 80.21% on Dataset 1 (4-class tasks), 90.19% on Dataset 2 (2-class tasks), and 97.32% on Dataset 3 (4-class tasks), surpassing the strongest baselines FBCNet on Dataset 1, MSFBCNN on Dataset 2 and MSFBCNN on Dataset 3 by 2.59%, 1.27%, and 1.99% respectively. The network effectively decoded the MI-based EEG signals, providing a potential method for BCI applications.

papers.title: Sleep in Different Types of Dizziness.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and dizziness are frequently comorbid, yet the specific sleep profiles across different vestibular disorders remain poorly characterized. This study aimed to investigate distinct sleep signatures in patients with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), vestibular migraine (VM), and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) compared to healthy controls. We conducted a cross-sectional study with 90 participants: 24 healthy controls, 21 with BPPV, 23 with PPPD, and 22 with VM. Sleep was assessed using a multimodal approach: 14-day actigraphy, a single-night home sleep apnea test (Watch-PAT), and validated questionnaires, including the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI), and Beck Anxiety/Depression Inventories. All dizziness groups reported significantly worse subjective sleep quality and higher psychological burden than controls. However, each disorder presented a unique objective signature: BPPV: Characterized by objective sleep fragmentation and a markedly higher Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI: 31.5) and Oxygen Desaturation Index (ODI: 16). These patients also showed increased nocturnal restlessness (L5). PPPD: Demonstrated a "sleep paradox" with the highest objective sleep efficiency but the poorest subjective perception (PSQI: 11.0). Patients showed reduced daytime activity (M10) and rigid sleep routines with virtually no weekend-weekday get-up time difference. VM: Distinguished by the shortest total sleep time and pronounced, though not statistically significant, "social jetlag", reflected by a 120-min discrepancy between weekend and weekday get-up times. Dizziness is not a homogeneous entity regarding sleep. The distinct signatures found suggest that clinical management should be tailored: screening for sleep apnea in BPPV, addressing the objective-subjective disconnect in PPPD via cognitive-behavioral approaches, and managing sleep deprivation and circadian regularity in VM.

papers.title: Noninvasive respiratory therapy: A physiology-oriented approach across acute, chronic, home, and palliative care settings.
papers.abstract: Noninvasive respiratory therapy has evolved from a strategy used to avoid endotracheal intubation in selected forms of acute respiratory failure into a broader framework encompassing acute care, chronic respiratory failure, sleep-disordered breathing, home respiratory support, pulmonary rehabilitation, and palliative care. The term now encompasses conventional oxygen therapy, high-flow nasal cannula therapy, continuous positive airway pressure, bilevel noninvasive ventilation, home noninvasive ventilation, home high-flow therapy, and positive airway pressure therapy for sleep-related breathing disorders. This review proposes a physiology-oriented approach. Rather than selecting a device solely according to the disease, clinicians should identify the dominant physiological problem: impaired oxygenation, alveolar hypoventilation, upper-airway obstruction, increased work of breathing, respiratory muscle fatigue, impaired secretion clearance, or the need for comfort-oriented support. In acute care, noninvasive ventilation is well established for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure due to COPD exacerbations and for acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, whereas high-flow nasal cannula therapy, continuous positive airway pressure, and noninvasive ventilation require more careful selection in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. In chronic care, home noninvasive ventilation and home high-flow therapy should be understood as components of long-term respiratory care systems rather than as simple device prescriptions. Practical success depends on appropriate interface selection, leak control, humidification, patient-device synchrony, airway clearance, patient education, and safe monitoring. A physiology-oriented and patient-centered framework may improve the appropriate use of noninvasive respiratory therapy across the continuum of care.

papers.title: EEG Biomarkers for Rett Syndrome: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning and Deep Learning with Explainable AI
papers.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by abnormal cortical activity, which can be captured using electroencephalography (EEG). Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise for diagnosing several neurological conditions, comprehensive evaluation of classical ML and deep learning (DL) methods, together with physiologically meaningful explanations, remains limited for RTT. This study analyses resting-state, eyes-closed EEG recordings from RTT patients and healthy controls using both power spectral density (PSD)-based ML and end-to-end DL frameworks. Classical ML models, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and XGBoost, were trained on PSD features, while EEG-specific DL architectures, including ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet, EEGNet, and EEG Conformer, were trained directly on preprocessed EEG signals. Subject-wise cross-validation was used to avoid data leakage, with balanced accuracy as the primary performance metric because it equally accounts for sensitivity and specificity. Random Forest achieved the best performance among the classical ML models, whereas EEGNet achieved the highest DL performance. An ablation study indicated that 4-second EEG epochs offered the optimal trade-off between model performance and robustness. Model interpretability was investigated using SHAP for Random Forest and occlusion sensitivity analysis for EEGNet. Both methods consistently identified delta and theta oscillations, along with centro-frontal brain regions, as key contributors to RTT classification. These findings show that both PSD-based machine learning and end-to-end deep learning methods can reliably identify RTT and highlight common neurophysiological biomarkers, offering an interpretable framework for EEG-based diagnosis and biomarker discovery for Rett Syndrome.

papers.title: Influence of chiropractic care on sleep-related behavior of athletic Mangalarga Marchador horses.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental biological process for homeostasis in mammals. Chiropractic is a manual therapeutic approach that aims to restore joint mobility, correct biomechanical dysfunctions, and optimize welfare. The present study examined the influence of chiropractic sessions on resting behavior patterns of Mangalarga Marchador horses raised in an intensive system. Nine Mangalarga Marchador horses, with an average age of 4.2 ± 1.2 years, were evaluated for their sleep-related behavior over 72 hours, followed by a chiropractic session, and reassessed over the next 72 hours post-session. After 35 days, horses received a second chiropractic session and were observed for another 72 hours, pre- and post-session. There was a reduction in wakefulness time (Pre: 1,128.22±32.02; Post: 1,063.66±29.16 min, p=0.003) and an increase in time in lateral recumbency after the chiropractic sessions (1st: from 129.24±43.88 min to 147.14±46.25 min and 2nd: from 88.55±28.19 min to 143.10±38.58 min, p=0.004). These results suggest that chiropractic care is associated with changes in sleep-related behavior in athletic horses. Further studies using electroencephalography are needed to determine whether these behavioral changes are associated with alterations in sleep physiology.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence applications in intracranial electroencephalography for epilepsy management: Insights from AI in Epilepsy 2025.
papers.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) provides direct recordings of cortical activity and remains central to the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, the high dimensionality and complexity of iEEG data increasingly challenge conventional visual interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods have accelerated quantitative analyses in electrophysiology, supporting localization, outcome prediction, and therapeutic decision-making in epilepsy. This article reviews recent advances in the application of AI to iEEG in epilepsy and in particular stereo-EEG, although the concepts discussed are broadly relevant across iEEG modalities. Although many of these approaches have shown encouraging results, the current evidence remains largely preliminary, with most studies being retrospective, single-center investigations that lack independent external validation. AI-based integration of iEEG with multimodal magnetic resonance imaging shows promise for improving surgical planning in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Concurrently, early studies suggest that AI-driven iEEG analysis may enhance epileptogenic zone identification by detecting subtle electrophysiological signatures, network interactions, and temporal dynamics. These multimodal frameworks emphasize distributed epileptic networks rather than isolated focal abnormalities. AI is also reshaping how iEEG-guided stimulation is designed and interpreted. Data-driven approaches have the potential to optimize stimulation parameters, predict network responses, and clarify mechanisms underlying diagnostic and therapeutic stimulation, laying the groundwork for adaptive, patient-specific neuromodulation. Beyond short-term epilepsy monitoring, AI applications increasingly incorporate continuous sensing, longitudinal network modeling, and integration with implantable neurotechnology platforms. Although these developments require prospective multicenter studies with external validation before widespread clinical implementation, advances in multimodal data integration, interpretable modeling, and continuous sensing position AI-enhanced iEEG as an emerging platform for precision brain network medicine for epilepsy.

papers.title: Perioperative Neurocognitive Disorders in Older Adults: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Evidence-Informed Management.
papers.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PNDs) encompass cognitive change identified before or after surgery. Postoperative delirium (POD) is an acute, fluctuating disorder of attention and awareness, whereas delayed neurocognitive recovery and postoperative mild or major neurocognitive disorder describe objectively assessed decline over longer intervals. This narrative review focuses on older adults undergoing noncardiac and cardiac surgery and examines neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, neurotransmitter imbalance, oxidative stress, synaptic dysfunction, candidate fluid biomarkers, and electroencephalography (EEG) features, and evidence-informed management. Multicomponent prevention, medication review, mobilization, sleep support, and individualized anesthetic care remain the most defensible clinical strategies. EEG-guided anesthetic titration can reduce anesthetic exposure but has not consistently reduced POD. Blood biomarkers, machine-learning models, trial-by-trial neural variability, and noninvasive brain stimulation are promising research tools, but none currently replaces standardized clinical assessment or justifies routine mechanism-specific treatment.

papers.title: Metabolic Dyshomeostasis, neuroinflammation, and glymphatic clearance deficits as convergent drivers of Alzheimer's disease: an exposome-based conceptual framework for prevention.
papers.abstract: The repeated failures of anti-amyloid therapies in Alzheimer's disease (AD) have exposed critical limitations of the linear amyloid cascade hypothesis and underscored the need for a broader etiological framework. The objective of this review is to synthesise mechanistic evidence for an exposome‑based model of sporadic AD that integrates metabolic, inflammatory, and sleep/circadian contributions to brain aging. Epidemiological evidence indicates that up to 40% of AD risk is attributable to modifiable environmental and lifestyle factors. These factors, collectively termed the aging exposome, represent the cumulative measure of external exposures and the body's biological responses across the lifespan. The central hypothesis is that sporadic AD emerges from the synergistic convergence of three interconnected exposome domains, metabolic dyshomeostasis, chronic neuroinflammation, and sleep/circadian disruption, which collectively lower the threshold for clinical dementia through shared molecular hubs like NF‑κB, mTOR, and ER stress. Central to this model is brain insulin resistance, which impairs cerebral glucose utilization, compromises mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, and disrupts lipid homeostasis via ceramide/sphingomyelin imbalance, collectively driving bioenergetic failure, oxidative stress, and enhanced amyloid-β production. Concurrently, peripherally derived and central inflammatory signals prime microglia, upregulate β-secretase (BACE1), and activate complement-mediated synaptic pruning, while emerging evidence suggests that sleep fragmentation and circadian misalignment are hypothesized to reduce glymphatic clearance and sustain BACE1 elevation, although direct causal evidence in humans remains limited. These ostensibly disparate pathways are integrated by shared molecular hubs, NF-κB, mTOR, and endoplasmic reticulum stress, which establish a self-reinforcing vicious cycle that selectively damages the hippocampus and default mode network. This cumulative aging exposome burden exerts its greatest impact during the midlife metabolic storm window (ages 40-60) and exhibits sex-specific vulnerability. Collectively, metabolic, inflammatory, and sleep deficits amplify each other via shared hubs; midlife is a critical, sex‑specific vulnerability window; and multi‑domain prevention is rational, though causal proof requires exposome‑wide and pragmatic trials. This reframes sporadic AD as an exposome‑driven syndrome, favoring simultaneous metabolic, immune, and sleep interventions over single‑target approaches.

papers.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients
papers.abstract: Background: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. Methods: We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. Results: ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

papers.title: Home non-invasive ventilation in chronic respiratory failure: Evidence-based guidelines.
papers.abstract: Home non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is used across a range of causes of chronic respiratory failure, but patient selection and management are disease-specific. These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations on initiating, titrating, and monitoring long-term home NIV across different disease spectrums. The panel reviewed studies from international databases, relevant guidelines, and reference lists. The panel refined recommendations through two rounds of consensus and graded them using the Indian Chest Society framework. In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), home NIV is recommended for eligible patients with persistent daytime hypercapnia, including those who remain hypercapnic 2 to 4 weeks after an exacerbation. High-intensity bilevel ventilation should be titrated to achieve a meaningful reduction in arterial carbon dioxide. In neuromuscular disorders, respiratory muscle weakness or hypoventilation warrants timely assessment for NIV, alongside evaluation of interface tolerance and secretion clearance. For stable obesity hypoventilation syndrome with severe obstructive sleep apnoea, continuous positive airway pressure is generally the preferred initial treatment; NIV is appropriate when severe obstructive sleep apnoea is absent or continuous positive airway pressure fails or is not tolerated. The guidelines also address heart failure with sleep-disordered breathing, chest-wall deformity, interstitial lung disease, bronchiectasis, post-tuberculosis lung disease, central hypoventilation syndromes, and palliative care. Across indications, management should include individualised ventilator settings, objective assessment of ventilation, patient and caregiver education, and structured follow-up. Where evidence is limited, recommendations reflect expert consensus and should be applied in the context of patient goals, clinical feasibility, and available resources.

papers.title: Trajectories of postoperative fatigue and their association with physical and mental health among patients with peritoneal metastases from colorectal and appendiceal cancer after cytoreductive surgery and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy: a 1-year longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: Postoperative fatigue (POF) is a common complication following major or medium-sized surgeries. It is influenced by surgical trauma, pain, sleep quality, nutrition, and mental state, and can significantly hinder postoperative recovery. As enhanced recovery protocols become more widely adopted in perioperative care, attention to the prevention and management of POF has increased. This 1-year longitudinal study enrolled patients with peritoneal metastases from colorectal and appendiceal cancer following cytoreductive surgery and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (CRS-HIPEC) at two tertiary hospitals. Participants completed self-administered questionnaires at discharge, and at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months after surgery. POF was assessed using the 10-item Identity-Consequence Fatigue Scale (ICFS-10). Group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) was utilized to identify distinct POF trajectories, and multivariable models were fitted to examine their associations with sleep quality, pain, and physical and mental conditions over time. The reporting of this study adhered to the Guidelines for Reporting on Latent Trajectory Studies (GRoLTS) checklist. Among 182 participants who experienced POF during follow-up, three distinct fatigue trajectories were identified: high-increasing (29.67%), moderate-increasing (37.36%), and low-increasing (31.87%). Poor sleep quality, inadequate pain management, and compromised physical and mental conditions were linked to trajectory groups with more severe fatigue symptoms. After adjusting for covariates, the high-increasing trajectory group demonstrated significantly lower scores in mental dimensions at 12 months post-discharge. This study presents the cumulative incidence and longitudinal trajectories of POF over a 1-year postoperative period, analyzing the relationship between physical and mental conditions in peritoneal metastatic cancer survivors. Our findings underscore the importance of early identification and targeted treatment of high-risk patients to prevent the chronic progression of POF. These trajectory patterns provide potential clinical avenues for the early detection and management of persistent fatigue based on a patient's evolving symptom profile.

papers.title: Circadian-Psychosocial Profiling of Cancer Pain: A Mixed-Methods Study on Heterogeneous Subgroups and Personalized Analgesic Efficacy.
papers.abstract: To identify distinct cancer pain subgroups using integrated circadian, physiological and psychosocial data and assess subgroup-specific analgesic responses. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study included 191 adult inpatients with cancer pain from a tertiary care hospital. Quantitative measures included 24-h blood pressure, salivary melatonin, pain beliefs, coping styles, social support, and clinical variables. Mixed-type cluster analysis (K-prototypes) identified subgroups. Analgesic efficacy was evaluated using multiple linear regression, with changes in mean pain intensity and pain variability as the outcomes. The qualitative phase involved semi-structured interviews analyzed thematically. Four distinct patient subgroups (Cluster 0-3) were identified. Cluster 0 (elderly reverse-dipper, n = 44) showed moderate pain, poor sleep quality, emotional lability, and social withdrawal. Analgesics exerted no significant effect on mean pain intensity (coefficient = 0.063, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.585 to 0.711, p = 0.856) or pain variability (coefficient = -1.466, 95% CI: -4.178 to 1.246, p = 0.335). Cluster 1 (non-dipper severe pain, n = 54) exhibited disrupted circadian rhythm, negative pain cognition, and avoidant coping. Analgesics significantly reduced pain variability (coefficient = -2.333, 95% CI: -4.001 to -0.665, p = 0.008) but not mean pain intensity (coefficient = 0.072, 95% CI: -0.300 to 0.444, p = 0.712). Cluster 2 (dipper mild pain, n = 74) maintained normal circadian rhythm, positive mental status, and active social interaction. Analgesics significantly decreased pain variability (coefficient = -3.427, 95% CI: -5.391 to -1.463, p = 0.002) but not mean pain intensity (coefficient = -0.248, 95% CI: -0.682 to 0.186, p = 0.274). Cluster 3 (high-melatonin, n = 19) achieved significant reductions in mean pain intensity (coefficient = -1.259, 95% CI: -2.031 to -0.487, p = 0.001) and pain variability (coefficient = -5.602, 95% CI: -8.664 to -2.540, p = 0.001), with passive coping and emotional suppression. Patients with cancer pain exhibit marked heterogeneity in circadian rhythm, endocrine function, and psychosocial profiles. Interactions among these factors may contribute to distinct pain mechanisms and variable analgesic responses. Comprehensive multidimensional assessment may facilitate more accurate patient subtyping and support individualized pain management. This study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) under registration number ChiCTR2500096806.

papers.title: A proposed psychometabolic endotype of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome: bidirectional interplay between psychological distress, eating dysfunction, sleep disruption, chronic stress, and metabolic deterioration.
papers.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome was renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) in 2026 to better represent its multisystem biology. Psychological distress, eating dysregulation, sleep disturbance, and metabolic dysfunction frequently coexist, yet clinical care and research commonly treat them as parallel comorbidities. To define the proposed psychometabolic construct operationally; position it relative to conventional phenotypes and data-driven clusters; and grade evidence for association, temporal prediction, causation, and treatment response across psychological, behavioral, sleep-stress, neuroendocrine, and metabolic pathways. We conducted a targeted narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE from inception through 15 September 2026. Seven structured topic blocks returned 1,278 records, 1,009 unique identifiers after PubMed identifier (PMID)-based deduplication, and 1,008 retrievable article records for title/abstract screening. Guidelines, systematic reviews, longitudinal or causal studies, trials, and informative human mechanistic studies were prioritized; general-population and preclinical evidence was used only when its indirectness was explicit. Depression and anxiety, body-image concerns, binge- and bulimia-spectrum symptoms, poor sleep, and obstructive sleep apnea are reported more often in PMOS than in comparison populations, but most estimates are cross-sectional and heterogeneous. One tertiary cohort found that baseline depression and/or anxiety history predicted incident metabolic syndrome over a median seven years (adjusted hazard ratio 1.45, 95% confidence interval 1.02-2.06); this supports prognostic enrichment, not causality. General-population longitudinal and genetic studies support reciprocal depression-metabolic relationships, whereas PMOS-specific causal evidence is inconsistent. Plausible links include insulin-androgen-adipose interactions, neuroactive steroid signaling, ovarian sympathetic input, sleep fragmentation, stress and autonomic regulation, reward-related eating, treatment exposure, stigma, and social context. None validates a discrete endotype. We define a candidate psychometabolic endotype as a cross-cutting, mechanistically coupled pattern that may occur within any conventional PMOS phenotype. Clinical co-occurrence is only an entry profile; endotype status requires replicated longitudinal coupling, incremental prognostic value, interpretable transitions, and preferably treatment-effect heterogeneity. Four overlapping prototypes are working formulations rather than subtypes. A six-step clinical pathway centers shared formulation and nests care-intensity tiers within treatment selection.

papers.title: Characterizing Cancer Symptom Experiences and Related Psychosocial Concerns Through Chinese Social Media Narratives: Computational Text Analysis.
papers.abstract: Patients with cancer frequently experience complex and multidimensional symptom burdens. Standardized patient-reported outcome measures provide structured approaches to symptom assessment but may not capture the full range of symptom-related and psychosocial concerns expressed in patients' narratives. Patient-generated social media data offer a complementary source for examining how these concerns are expressed online. This study aimed to characterize cancer symptom-related narratives in Chinese social media posts using a conventional symptom assessment framework and to identify additional experiential themes through neural topic modeling. A computational text analysis integrating large language model (LLM) annotation and neural topic modeling was conducted. A corpus of 26,086 first-person patient narratives was collected from Xiaohongshu and Zhihu between November 2013 and February 2026 using cancer-related search terms. First-person narratives and 6 SPPADE (sleep disturbance, pain, physical function impairment, anxiety, depression, and low energy or fatigue) symptom domains were identified using GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI) and validated against independent human coding. Symptom occurrence, co-occurrence, multiplicity, and coping strategies were characterized, with exploratory stratified analyses by cancer type. BERTopic modeling was applied to identify latent themes, platform sensitivity analyses, and temporal distribution were examined. For first-person narrative identification, human raters showed 89.2% agreement (Cohen κ=0.784); the LLM achieved an F1-score of 81.2% against the adjudicated reference standard. For SPPADE extraction, mean Cohen κ values for LLM-human agreement were 0.714 (SD 0.114) and 0.754 (SD 0.095) across the 6 symptom domains. Overall, 13,896 of 26,086 (53.3%) posts contained at least 1 identifiable symptom. Pain was the most frequently identified symptom (5783/26,086, 22.2%), followed by physical function impairment (4153/26,086, 15.9%) and depression (4050/26,086, 15.5%). Pain and physical function impairment formed the most frequent co-occurring symptom pair (n=1407). Coping strategies were described in 7104/26,086 (27.2%) posts; medication-based approaches were most prominent, particularly for pain and sleep disturbance, while social and psychological support were more common for anxiety and depression. BERTopic modeling identified 13 latent themes, including cancer treatment trajectories, health care system interaction, existential distress, family involvement, and financial burden, highlighting experiential concerns that may be underrepresented in conventional symptom assessment. The proportion of posts containing at least 1 SPPADE symptom was similar between Xiaohongshu and Zhihu (53.2% vs 54.1%; P=.35), although individual symptom distributions differed across platforms. Chinese social media posts contained multidimensional symptom-related narratives alongside psychosocial and experiential concerns that may be less visible in structured symptom assessment. Patient-generated social media data may therefore provide a complementary source for understanding cancer symptom experiences and supportive care concerns. However, differences in platform composition, uneven temporal coverage, and the nonrepresentativeness of social media users limit generalizability, and the clinical utility of integrating such data into routine symptom assessment requires further evaluation.

papers.title: [Pseudo-remission in childhood absence epilepsy. Objective assessment of seizure control and the role of ethosuximide].
papers.abstract: Absence epilepsy is a common form of pseudo-remission, in which patients and observers may incorrectly believe seizures have ceased while paroxysms persist in subtle form. Three primary factors contribute to this phenomenon: the brief duration (typically less than 10 seconds) and indistinct semiology of typical absences; the limited reliability of parental observation (sensitivity up to 43%); and the occurrence of generalized spike-wave discharges without significant clinical manifestations, which are nonetheless associated with fluctuations in wakefulness. Verification of remission requires at least a properly conducted three-minute hyperventilation test with attentional load. Preferred methods for objective assessment include prolonged video-EEG monitoring that registers wakefulness, sleep, and arousal, and, when indicated, intermittent photic stimulation. However, no direct comparative studies have demonstrated superiority of these methods over short-term EEG with adequately performed hyperventilation. Extended EEG monitoring does not substitute for the induction of provoking factors, and functional testing does not obviate the need for sufficient recording duration. The absence of "peak-slow wave" discharges lasting three seconds or longer may serve as a practical operational criterion, as adopted from the CAE study protocol. Data are presented on the proportion of patients free from treatment failure with ethosuximide, valproic acid, and lamotrigine in patients with newly diagnosed childhood absence epilepsy at Week 16 (53%, 58%, and 29%, respectively) and at Month 12 (45%, 44%, and 21%, respectively). The review also describes the mechanism of action of ethosuximide, discrepancies between NICE recommendations and Russian clinical guidelines, dosing considerations, and the need for laboratory monitoring. The clinical benefit of adjusting therapy based on EEG findings in patients with apparent clinical well-being remains unproven.

papers.title: Exploratory data analysis and machine learning-based assessment of social media addiction and its impact on academic performance and mental health among students.
papers.abstract: This study investigates social media addiction among students. It includes definitions, ways to measure it, how common it is, and its effects on mental health and academic performance. A focused review of literature from 2018 to 2025 gathers systematic reviews, meta-analyses, psychometric studies, and research that connects problematic social media use to issues like mental health problems, sleep disruptions, and academic results. The article also provides a method for analyzing student-level social media addiction data. It discusses common findings in datasets and offers recommendations for educators and policymakers based on evidence. Using data from 705 participants across 110 countries, this study combines a thorough literature review, dataset-driven exploratory data analysis (EDA), and correlational modeling. The results show strong connections between social media addiction, academic success, sleep, and mental health. The EDA reveals gender differences in usage, regional differences in platform preferences, and clear links between addiction and poorer sleep quality and mental health. These findings align with global research and suggest the potential value of targeted digital well-being interventions among students.

papers.title: NaV1.8 Inhibition and the Future of Nonopioid Analgesia in Otolaryngology: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Postoperative pain management in otolaryngology requires balancing effective analgesia while minimizing adverse effects, such as opioid-related complications. Suzetrigine is a first-in-class selective voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV1.8) inhibitor that has been recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration. Suzetrigine selectively inhibits NaV1.8 channels expressed in peripheral nociceptive neurons, thereby reducing pain signaling without the respiratory depression, sedation, or misuse potential associated with opioids. This review summarizes the pharmacology, efficacy, safety profile, limitations, and potential applications of suzetrigine in otolaryngology. Prospective clinical trials consist of 2 phase 2 randomized clinical trials, 2 phase 3 randomized placebo-controlled trials, and 1 phase 3 open-label study involving more than 3000 patients. Across abdominoplasty and bunionectomy pain models, suzetrigine demonstrated superior analgesia compared with placebo and mixed efficacy comparable to hydrocodone/acetaminophen. The drug was generally well tolerated, with adverse event rates similar to placebo and no significant respiratory, cardiac, or sedating adverse effects reported. Additionally, 1 retrospective cohort study has reported results in patients undergoing free flap reconstruction and transoral robotic surgery. Suzetrigine is a promising nonopioid analgesic with demonstrated efficacy compared to placebo in acute postoperative pain and a favorable safety profile. In otolaryngology, suzetrigine may serve as an adjunct to multimodal analgesia and an opioid-sparing option for patients with contraindications to traditional analgesics, opioid use disorder, or procedures that are expected to have high opioid utilization such as tonsillectomy, sleep surgery, and major head and neck surgery. Future studies in otolaryngology are warranted to evaluate whether suzetrigine can meaningfully reduce postoperative opioid exposure without compromising analgesic effectiveness.

papers.title: Rapid Improvement of Persistent Catatonia Temporally Associated With Amantadine After Benzodiazepine Intolerance and Discontinuation of Electroconvulsive Therapy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Catatonia can be difficult to manage when benzodiazepines are poorly tolerated, and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) cannot be continued. We report the case of a 23-year-old woman with a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder and catatonia presenting with mutism, delayed responses, staring, posturing, waxy flexibility, withdrawal, and abnormal behavior. Treatment with lorazepam was limited by excessive sedation. She then received four bitemporal ECT sessions before she and her mother declined further ECT due to reported adverse effects. Soon after discharge, she was found wandering outside while confused and required readmission. Nine days after her last ECT session, her Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) severity score was 11. Amantadine 100 mg twice daily was started, and three days later her BFCRS severity score fell to 3, a 72.7% reduction. Because her altered mental status persisted, a neurologic evaluation was performed. Brain MRI, routine electroencephalography (EEG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies, infectious testing, and neuronal autoantibody testing, including N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antibody testing, were unremarkable. Amantadine was then increased to 200 mg twice daily, and zolpidem 5 mg nightly was later added. Her final BFCRS severity score was 2. Although delayed ECT effects, concurrent treatment of the underlying psychotic disorder, spontaneous fluctuation, and subsequent interventions preclude causal attribution, this case shows rapid, objectively measured improvement temporally associated with the start of amantadine treatment.

papers.title: Neuronal intermediate filament neurologic autoimmunity in a patient with Merkel cell carcinoma receiving pembrolizumab.
papers.abstract: Neuronal intermediate filament (NIF) autoimmunity is an uncommon paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome that has increasingly been recognized in association with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. Merkel cell carcinoma is among the malignancies most frequently associated with NIF antibodies, although reported cases remain limited. A 55-year-old female with stage IIIA Merkel cell carcinoma developed vertigo, gait instability, dysarthria, and persistent right hemifacial and cervical spasms after receiving second dose of pembrolizumab for recurrent disease. Brain MRI was unremarkable, while continuous electroencephalography demonstrated encephalopathy without a definitive electrocerebral correlate, raising suspicion for subcortical myoclonus. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein. CSF and positive NIF antibodies using cell-based assay. Pembrolizumab was discontinued, and the patient was treated with high-dose corticosteroids followed by monthly intravenous immunoglobulin, resulting in near complete resolution of her neurologic symptoms after 6 months. This case expands the growing spectrum of ICI-associated NIF paraneoplastic neurologic autoimmunity complicating Merkel cell carcinoma. To our knowledge, persistent hemifacial and cervical spasm has rarely been reported in this clinical setting. Early recognition of this syndrome, prompt antibody testing, discontinuation of ICI therapy, and initiation of therapy may improve neurological outcomes while informing further oncologic management.
